similar_scenes.name: Bebop: Charlie Parker y Dizzy Gillespie
similar_scenes.author: Ted Gioia
similar_scenes.desc: El jazz siempre fue moderno, pero el jazz moderno no nace de Ellington ni de Goodman en el Carnegie Hall, sino de jam sessions nocturnas de músicos de grupo (el guitarrista de Goodman, el bajista de Ellington, el saxo de Hines, el trompetista de Calloway): un movimiento underground que inaugura la mentalidad de búnker del jazz progresista. Nuevas melodías sobre los acordes de viejos standards, combos con saxo y trompeta al unísono, solos rapidísimos de corcheas regulares que empiezan y acaban en partes débiles, notas de tensión, sustituciones II-V, y una sección rítmica heredera de Kansas City con «bombas» de batería (Kenny Clarke, Max Roach). Charlie Parker, formado con Buster Smith y Jay McShann y en los discos de Lester Young, une el blues de Kansas City con Stravinsky y Hindemith; Dizzy Gillespie, heredero de Roy Eldridge y alumno de Mario Bauza, es el virtuoso y el showman. En 1945 graban para Guild y Savoy («Groovin' High», «Salt Peanuts», «Ko Ko»); Parker se hunde en California (la sesión de «Lover Man», Camarillo), vuelve con un estilo más relajado («Embraceable You», «Parker's Mood») y muere en 1955 con treinta y cuatro años y el cuerpo de un hombre de sesenta. Para los músicos negros, el bebop es también la exigencia de ser reconocidos como artistas.

podcast.title: Colloquial Usage in 1956
podcast.body: By 1956, the term "Bbapp" had acquired a distinct, colloquial meaning for most people, divergent from its precise jazz definition. It generally meant "that noisy music I don't understand that the young people like," often associated with black artists. This broader usage encompassed rhythm and blues, rock and roll, and rockabilly, illustrating a rapid cultural shift in terminology. "Colloquially, Bbapp meant, that noisy music I don't understand that the young people like, and most of the people making it a black."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" Naming Convention
podcast.body: Despite having minimal musical connection to jazz bebop, the name "Be-Bop-A-Lula" still fit the colloquial understanding of "bop" in 1956. At that time, "bop" was a catch-all term for youth-oriented, "noisy music," making the title culturally relevant even without direct jazz influence. "So even though Bbappalula had about as much to do with Bbapp as it did with Stravinsky, the name still fit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Birth During Strike
podcast.body: Bebop, or just bop, was a new and highly important form of jazz invented in New York between 1942 and 1944 by musicians like Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. These artists played in big bands but were also developing this innovative style in their side gigs. Tragically for music lovers, the Musicians' Union Strike of 1942-44 meant that there are no recordings of bebop's crucial birth period, making its early evolution historically elusive. "There was a new form of jazz being invented in New York between 1942 and 1944, by musicians like Deseagle S.P. and Charlie Parker, people who played in the big bands but were also doing something new in their side gigs."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 2: "Roll Em Pete" by Big Joe Turner

podcast.title: Birth in the 1940s
podcast.body: Bebop emerged in the 1940s as a new form of rhythmic popular music. Its development was driven by the impracticality of maintaining large, expensive big bands, particularly after World War II, necessitating smaller ensembles that could deliver more volume and power with fewer musicians. "A new form of rhythmic popular music called Bebop was being born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Emergence as a Jazz Splinter (WWII Era)
podcast.body: Bebop emerged during World War II as a splintering of the traditional jazz sound. Ambitious musicians, tired of the rigid structure of Big Bands, would gather after gigs for long nights of improvisational jams. This resulted in an experimental, very complex, and virtuosic style created by musicians for musicians, often without a discernible beat or melody for dancing. "The result was a splintering of the jazz sound into something that became known as bebop, experimental, very complex virtuosity made by musicians for musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution into Rhythm and Blues
podcast.body: Bebop eventually evolved into what became known as rhythm and blues, marking a significant transition in popular music. "This evolved into what became known as rhythm and blues, and this is key."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Original Definition (Mid-1940s)
podcast.body: The term "Bebop," as it originated in New York in the mid-1940s, specifically referred to a style of jazz music that prioritized "harmonic complexity, instrumental virtuosity, and individual self-expression." This genre was famously performed by musicians such as Charlie Parker, Oscar Peterson, Dexter Gordon, and Dizzy Gillespie, effectively defining jazz in the post-war era. "The term Bbapp, as it was originally used, was used in the same way we use it now, for a type of jazz music that originated in New York in the mid-1940s, which prized harmonic complexity, instrumental virtuosity, and individual self-expression."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Pioneered by Louis Jordan
podcast.body: Bandleader Louis Jordan is credited with pioneering Bebop, characterized by his insistence on heavy shuffle rhythms. This stylistic choice was a key factor in the genre's evolution. "Band leader Louis Jordan pioneered Bebop, insisting on heavy shuffle rhythms."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Rise in the 1940s
podcast.body: Following the decline of big bands in the 1940s, bebop became a genre that young people gravitated towards, alongside R&B, the blues, and country western. This marked a generational shift in musical preference, moving away from older styles.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Role in Big Band Decline
podcast.body: The rise of bebop, with its complex and un-danceable nature, appealed to musicians seeking artistic freedom and challenge, and its pioneers like Charlie Parker and Miles Davis contributed to the decline of the more commercially focused big bands. "Their work helped put the nail in the coffin of the big bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
